listenings.text: I have moderated conferences for about ten years, and I always ask the speakers the same thing before we start. Please, give me one minute, not five. The most common mistake is when a speaker reads their whole CV, with every job and every date. The audience stops listening after the second company. So I ask for three things. First, what you do now. Second, one thing you did before that explains your experience. And third, why you are on this panel today. That is all. When a speaker gives me those three things, the introduction sounds natural, and the audience wants to hear more.

I worked at a law firm for twelve years, mostly in contracts. Then, in 2018, a client invited me to join the company as a director, and two years later I became the CEO. I stayed there until 2023. I stepped down because I wanted more time with my own clients, and because I missed legal work. Since then, I have advised about fifteen companies, most of them in energy and transport. People sometimes ask me if it was a mistake to leave the law for so long. I don't think so. Because I have sat on the other side of the table, I understand what the board is worried about, and not only the legal risk.

Foreign funds have invested more money in Latin American infrastructure over the last five years than in the ten years before. But when a fund looks at a new project, the first question is not about the road or the airport. It is about the rules. Who is the regulator, and how stable are the rules? Many concessions last twenty or thirty years, so a change in regulation can change the whole business. That is why investors want people on their team who understand both the law and the business, and who can explain one to the other.
